correspondence.component_scope: Palo Blanco opening and southward Santa Rita del Sotol approach
correspondence.finding: The chosen northern opening lies in the small drainage setting beside and northeast of Palo Blanco. The regional basin maps depict the receiving north–south valley and the southward connection beside Santa Rita del Sotol. The selected western turn and continuation can be located at ordinary corridor scale. The source does not provide a natural name for this opening or the receiving trunk; Palo Blanco and Santa Rita del Sotol are locality names, not river names.

correspondence.component_scope: Southward approach east of Cedral and tributary joins
correspondence.finding: The selected course bends southwest and then south along the valley east of Cedral, west of Guadalupe de los Faz. The acquired basin cartography shows successive eastern hillside drainages entering this receiving corridor and distinguishes the more westerly Cedral approach. Its generalized representation supports the ordinary valley continuation, without assigning a separate name to the selected trunk or every incoming stream. No content from the unavailable Cedral municipal original is used.

correspondence.component_scope: San Lorenzo and eastern Matehuala corridor
correspondence.finding: The selected south-running route passes west of the San Lorenzo locality and along the eastern side of the Matehuala setting. Both basin maps show the connected drainage and its joins from the western urban/plain side and eastern hills. The separately labeled Jaquis approach lies farther west; the selected route does not ascend that branch. No Jaquis name is transferred to the whole selection.

correspondence.component_scope: Maravillas and El Mezquite receiving valley
correspondence.finding: The selected mainstem continues south through the valley west of Maravillas and beside El Mezquite. The more detailed stream-order map shows its receiving drainage and repeated side-channel joins. The La Milpita label belongs to a western approach and does not establish the name of this long selected north–south route. No independently supported selected-river name was read.

correspondence.component_scope: San Gabriel convergence and accumulation setting
correspondence.finding: The route reaches the San Gabriel setting, where drainage from the northern valley meets the western and eastern approaches on the basin maps. The study includes a November 2014 field photograph of an impoundment in flood-prone ground at San Gabriel and describes endorheic accumulation. This supports the convergence and lowland setting, rather than a named lake transit or the subsequent long southward through-link.

correspondence.component_scope: South of San Gabriel toward El Milagro de Guadalupe
correspondence.finding: The selected line continues south across the broad interior plain toward the El Milagro de Guadalupe setting. The acquired stream-order and basin maps show distinct local branches, some ending on the plain, but do not establish the whole chosen southward through-channel from the San Gabriel convergence to the Milagro drainage. The general endorheic basin description and nearby road cannot supply that missing hydraulic/corridor connection. This is the principal material gap.

correspondence.component_scope: Stored final turn west of San José del Refugio
correspondence.finding: The actual stored final turn lies in the interior plain south of El Milagro de Guadalupe and west of San José del Refugio. The two basin maps and the Villa de Guadalupe relief map locate that setting. The report describes basin accumulation southwest of San José del Refugio, but does not identify the stored tip as a distinct named lake, reservoir or natural-channel terminus. Neither the prior San Gabriel lowland nor the locality named Presa de Maltos is substituted for the stored endpoint. The connection into this final plain remains unestablished.

correspondence.component_scope: Chosen western opening and east-southeast upper progression
correspondence.finding: The author-produced volcanic map covers the southern Mendoza volcanic-terrain setting of this selected interval. It has no depiction establishing the chosen opening or this selected drainage channel; an exact lava-unit association is not assigned.

correspondence.component_scope: Upper southward turn and approach to the long middle interval
correspondence.finding: The regional volcanic-terrain figure includes the broad setting of the selected southward turn. Its lava-unit boundaries do not establish a watercourse or the connection through the turn; an exact unit crossing is not assigned.

correspondence.component_scope: Long eastward middle interval through the basaltic plateau
correspondence.finding: The volcanic source covers the western La Pampa plateau surrounding this middle interval. Neither the mapped lava-flow names nor the regional slope description establishes the intervening selected surface-drainage through-links.

correspondence.component_scope: Southeast lower turn west of Puelén
correspondence.finding: The volcanic map covers the lower plateau; the CFI regional sampling map begins to provide eastern-sector context. They do not depict the complete selected approach as a named or continuously connected drainage.

correspondence.component_scope: Final south-southeast approach and actual terminal setting
correspondence.finding: The CFI regional map places the selected ending inland west-southwest of Puelén and north of the separately mapped La Salinilla. Its enlarged La Salinilla map does not reach the selected endpoint. A receiving-water identity and the final through-link remain unestablished; La Salinilla is not assigned as the terminal.

correspondence.component_scope: chosen mountain opening
correspondence.finding: The Comondú Relieve original depicts the selected small headward drainage near Cerro Picacho, descending into an eastward receiving channel before the turn toward the municipal boundary. The nearby parallel southern drainages remain distinct. The chosen point is a model opening on this mapped feeder, not a claim about the officially recognized source. No printed hydronym is securely assigned to the complete chosen opening.

correspondence.component_scope: eastern loop and boundary crossings
correspondence.finding: The paired municipal maps supply complementary coverage where Comondú clips the eastern circuit. Loreto depicts the stream entering its western mountain margin, turning north and then returning northwest toward Comondú. The joining reaches align across the two municipal footprints. This closes the intervening channel connection; it is not inferred from basin membership alone.

correspondence.component_scope: northern westward receiving corridor
correspondence.finding: Comondú depicts the northern receiving watercourse continuing west, with joining northern and southern mountain channels, then bending southwest to the southward valley. The selected northern bends and intervening joins follow this connected watercourse. The 1996 study independently describes an upper joined course, Las Cruces and other tributaries, followed by a westward reach and the La Pintada southward turn; its prose does not establish exact name-transition vertices.

correspondence.component_scope: southward valley and lower named course
correspondence.finding: The selected course turns south through the connected valley and then southwest into the channel directly labeled La Purísima by Comondú. The hydrological study identifies the same regional river and describes the southwestward continuation below San Isidro. Its Figure 5.3C distinguishes this drainage from the neighboring San Gregorio and Comondú watercourses.

correspondence.component_scope: lower plain joins and final turn
correspondence.finding: The municipal original depicts the lower joined channel crossing the plain, curving west and then south to the coast. The selection follows those connected lower reaches, including the final southward leg. No intervening lake, reservoir or unproved plain crossing is required to join the selected lower corridor to its coastal endpoint.

correspondence.component_scope: actual coastal terminal
correspondence.finding: The actual stored endpoint corresponds at ordinary map scale to the Pacific-side termination of the La Purísima corridor. Both the municipal original and hydrological Figure 5.3C carry the drainage to the Pacific coast. This finding concerns the selected coastal endpoint, not an earlier inland end or an extension to another bay. The source generalization does not establish a surveyed mouth position or contemporary shoreline.

correspondence.component_scope: waterbody and flow scope
correspondence.finding: The inspected maps establish an arid mountain-valley and coastal-plain stream system without a named reservoir, lake or glacier passage on the selection. Comondú’s table lists La Purísima as perennial and Loreto lists intermittent upper streams. Those historical classifications do not establish year-round water at every selected reach or present operating conditions.

correspondence.component_scope: Chosen western opening and upper glacial passage
correspondence.finding: The independent expedition account directly describes Elaho River emerging at the Elaho Glacier snout. Golder describes Elaho as a glacial stream. Neither establishes the selected opening, its initial bend and its through-link to the downstream selected valley. Remaining gap: Usable source depiction linking the actual selected opening across the glacier/proglacial setting into the upper Elaho channel. No intervening lake is asserted from uninspected cartography.

correspondence.component_scope: Upper and middle Elaho corridor, tributary junctions and lower canyon
correspondence.finding: Authorial project prose identifies a glacial Elaho River, its lower canyon and its connection to Squamish River. The restoration project identifies Sims Creek and Clendinning Creek as tributaries. Their separate names are not assigned to the selected trunk. The acquired prose does not continuously trace all selected upper and middle Elaho parts. Remaining gap: Independent readable corridor cartography covering the upper southeast reach, southward valley, intermediate tributary junctions and final Elaho approach.

correspondence.component_scope: Elaho–Squamish confluence and first fragment join
correspondence.finding: Golder independently states that Elaho joins Squamish River upstream of the lower watershed. This establishes the named tributary relationship but does not locate the selected join on usable inspected map pixels. The separate upper Squamish headwater branch is not substituted for the selected Elaho approach. Remaining gap: A usable map or equivalent primary geographic depiction of the selected confluence and its adjacent through-links.

correspondence.component_scope: Upper and middle receiving Squamish valley
correspondence.finding: Planning accounts describe the receiving Squamish valley, the upstream canyon, downstream braided-to-meandering progression and Ashlu contribution. Golder records a Cheakamus power diversion into Squamish. These are bounded corridor and managed-inflow context; no selected crossing of Daisy Reservoir or a powerhouse is inferred. Continuous selected correspondence north of the mapped District reach remains incomplete. Remaining gap: Independent usable depiction from the Elaho junction through the middle Squamish valley to the lower mapped reach, including significant junction settings.

correspondence.component_scope: Cheakamus confluence setting and Brackendale lower corridor
correspondence.finding: KWL Figure2-1 and the District2013 orthophoto-backed Figure5-3 depict the Cheakamus entry into the lower Squamish and the connected southward river corridor. The selected continuation follows Squamish, rather than the separate Cheakamus branch.

correspondence.component_scope: Second fragment join and lower river past Mamquam
correspondence.finding: The KWL location map and independently attributed District2013 orthophoto Figure5-1 show the connected Squamish reach and Mamquam confluence. The mapped lower-river alignment crosses the second stored fragment join without switching to Mamquam or the disconnected sloughs.

correspondence.component_scope: Diked lower channel, estuary and actual stored sea terminal
correspondence.finding: KWL Figure2-1 depicts Squamish continuing beside the training-berm/Spit corridor into Howe Sound; its estuary account describes the western main channel. DrawingSW6 supplies independent orthophoto-backed lower-channel context. This supports the selected ending at the estuary/Howe Sound interface. Scope: Historical2017 publication context, not a claim about present berm configuration, exact bank position, freshwater/tidal limit or flow operation.
correspondence.candidate_name: Squamish River; Howe Sound receiving inlet
